title: Ex 8.17 · Product distributes over intersection
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove that $A \times (B \cap C) = (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)$. The elements of these sets are ordered pairs, so follow a pair $(x, y)$.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A × (B ∪ C)) or a statement about an ordered pair (x, y) (like x ∈ A and y ∈ B, or (x, y) ∈ A × B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: (x, y) ∈ A × (B ∩ C) means x ∈ A and y ∈ B and y ∈ C.
x ∈ A is the same as (x ∈ A and x ∈ A), so you can use it twice.
Regroup as (x ∈ A and y ∈ B) and (x ∈ A and y ∈ C): each bracket is membership in a product.
solution: Let $(x, y)$ be any ordered pair. Then $(x, y) \in A \times (B \cap C)$ means $x \in A \land (y \in B \land y \in C)$.
Since $x \in A$ is equivalent to $x \in A \land x \in A$, we can regroup this as $(x \in A \land y \in B) \land (x \in A \land y \in C)$.
That says $(x, y) \in A \times B$ and $(x, y) \in A \times C$, so $(x, y) \in (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)$.
Every step was an equivalence, so $A \times (B \cap C) = (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the Cartesian product (Section 1.2) and the logic laws of Section 2.6. The book also works this identity as Examples 8.12 and 8.13.

steps.content: x ∈ A and (y ∈ B and y ∈ C)
(x ∈ A and y ∈ B) and (x ∈ A and y ∈ C)
(x, y) ∈ A × B and (x, y) ∈ A × C
x ∈ A and (y ∈ B and y ∈ C)
(x ∈ A and y ∈ B) or (x ∈ A and y ∈ C)
x ∈ A and (y ∈ B and y ∈ C)
